column4: The feeders say that they act only for God's face and want neither جَزَاءً nor thanks from the recipients, the closest parallel to giving without repaying or creating a human claim.
Spending is expressly for God's face, while every good expenditure is repaid to the giver; this transfers repayment from the human recipient to God.
The verse contrasts a gift intended to grow in other people's wealth with zakat intended for God's face, precisely separating interested transfer from unindebted giving.
Those who spend and do not follow the gift with reminder or injury refuse to turn their helping hand into a later claim on its recipient.
The command not to nullify charity with reminder and injury shows the section's benefaction becoming an instrument of debt and domination.
A contracted slave seeking freedom is to be contracted with and given وَءَاتُوهُم from the wealth God gave the owners, joining emancipatory striving, God's prior gift, and a liberating human hand.
The prescribed uses of alms include both freeing necks and debtors, placing the section's slavery and debt scenes inside one act of giving.
The parable opposes an owned slave who can do nothing to one whom God provided well and who spends secretly and openly, making freedom visible as the power to give.
فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ makes freeing a neck itself the steep moral ascent, directly realizing the section's slave working to unbind his neck.
Righteousness includes giving loved wealth and spending it فِى ٱلرِّقَابِ, so the generous hand directly becomes a means of emancipation.
Taking charity from wealth is said to purify and increase its givers, directly paralleling giving wealth in order to purify oneself.
Male and female almsgivers are described as lending God a good loan that He multiplies, joining charity, debt, and divine recompense without making a human recipient indebted.
The hand chained to the neck and the hand spread to its utmost are the Quran's bodily limits for the section's clenched and extended palm.
The claim that God's hand is fettered is answered with بَلْ يَدَاهُ مَبْسُوطَتَانِ and His free spending, making open and bound hands figures of bounty and stinginess.
The hypocrites قَبَضُوا أَيْدِيَهُمْ, a literalized withdrawal of their hands that stages the section's miserly closed palm.
What people withheld in stinginess will be placed around their necks, turning retained wealth into the bodily bond described in the prose.
After God gives them from His bounty, they become stingy and turn away; بَخِلُوا and تَوَلَّوا unite two of surah 92's roots in one failed response to a gift.
When summoned to spend, the miser harms only himself because God is rich and people are poor, exposing the closed hand's false self-sufficiency.
Those who are stingy, urge stinginess, and turn away meet the declaration that God is self-sufficient, again joining بخل and تولي around refusal to give.
The verse joins stinginess, urging it on others, and concealing what God gave from His bounty, contrasting the received divine hand with the withheld human one.
Were people pressed for their wealth, they would become stingy; the pressure of an exacting claimant elicits the section's clenched hand.
أَعْطَىٰ قَلِيلًا وَأَكْدَىٰ stages a hand that gives a little and then stops, a direct boundary case for the section's giving motion.
Humans would withhold even God's treasuries out of fear of spending, explicitly naming إِمْسَاك as the reflex behind the tight fist.
The faithful spend neither wastefully nor niggardly, locating the measured hand between the two bodily extremes of 17:29.
Pharaoh cites raising Moses as a child as a benefit now chargeable against him, opening the precise conversation in which nurture becomes debt.
Pharaoh adds Moses' past deed and calls him ungrateful, showing the creditor's accusation that converts former care into a claim; 26:18 supplies the claimed care.
Moses calls the claimed upbringing a نِعْمَةٌ Pharaoh holds over him and sets it against Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel, joining favor, reminder, and slavery explicitly.
People treat their submission as a favor owed by the Messenger, but the verse reverses the claim: God is the one who conferred the favor of guidance.
People of means are told not to stop supporting relatives and the poor after an offense but to pardon, preventing a benefaction from becoming retaliatory leverage.
The hypocrites propose withholding support until the Messenger's companions disperse, displaying the giving hand used as a means of control.
The ruined garden owner turns his empty palms over what he spent, the concrete image of a giving hand left with nothing when its worldly attachment collapses.
The camel's killer فَتَعَاطَىٰ فَعَقَرَ, using the section's secondary تعاطي motion for a wrongful reaching that culminates in seizure and violence.
Joseph's brothers arrive with poor merchandise and ask him to complete the measure and give charity, staging the requesting hand before one able to give.
The restrained poor do not ask people importunately and may be mistaken for self-sufficient, refining the section's image of the outstretched begging palm.
When good touches the anxious human he becomes مَنُوعًا, withholding it in the exact motion of the section's closing hand.
The worshippers recognize a fixed right in their wealth, denying that what leaves the giver's hand is merely optional leverage over another.
That recognized right belongs to the asker and deprived person, supplying the recipient's outstretched hand for the wealth named in 70:24.
Their wealth contains a right for the asker and the deprived, again treating giving as delivery of another's right rather than creation of a debt.
The command not to repel the asker governs the very begging hand developed by the section.
Failure even to urge feeding the poor makes withholding visible as a social act rather than a private grip on wealth.
Withholding ٱلْمَاعُونَ closes the hand even against small, ordinary assistance, a miniature form of the section's grasping palm.
Divine bounty is said to be in God's hand and He يُؤْتِيهِ to whom He wills, joining hand, favor, and giving in one formulation.
The repeated claim that bounty is in God's hand and He gives it as He wills identifies the ultimate hand behind every human benefaction.
Some Bedouins treat what they spend as a financial loss and wait for disaster to reverse their position, the interested calculation opposed to pure giving.
Others treat spending as a means of nearness to God and the Messenger's prayers, relocating the gift's aim from human repayment to God.
Hoarded gold and silver that are not spent in God's way embody wealth held tight instead of released.
The hoarded wealth of 9:34 is heated and branded onto foreheads, sides, and backs, making retained property become a bodily bond and punishment.
The fire calls the person who turned his back, linking the section's turning-away root with the fate of the closed hand.
The one called by the fire gathered and withheld wealth, completing in 70:17-18 the sequence of turning away, accumulation, and refusal to give.
The garden owners resolve that no poor person will enter upon them, using control of the harvest to close every requesting hand.
After the garden is destroyed, its owners call themselves deprived, reversing the positions of those who denied the poor in 68:24.
The perishing of Abu Lahab's two hands makes the hand itself answer for what it grasped and performed.
His wealth and acquisitions do not avail him, completing the ruined hands of 111:1 and closely echoing wealth that cannot save when one falls.
A human has only what he strives for, which recalls the slave's سعاية labor toward release while placing ownership in one's work rather than another's favor.
The striving of 53:39 will be seen, making the labor toward freedom and every other striving subject to divine witness rather than a human master's account.
That striving is then repaid with the fullest recompense, directly joining سعي and جزاء across 53:39-41.
Every soul is to be recompensed for what it strives, placing the section's سعي and جزاء together in a single divine accounting.
The good loan to God turns a creditor's world inside out: wealth leaves the human hand and God, who needs no loan, multiplies its return.
A good loan to God is multiplied and receives a noble reward, transferring collection and increase away from claims on needy recipients.
Lending God a good loan brings multiplication and forgiveness, again replacing a human debt bond with divine repayment.
The command to give zakat and lend God a good loan joins obligatory giving to the divine debtor metaphor without burdening a human recipient.
Israel's covenant joins zakat and a good loan to God, placing giving inside fidelity to God rather than a claim upon beneficiaries.
A debtor in hardship must receive respite until ease, and remission as charity is better; this directly reverses the dictionary's harsh creditor who refuses to wait for ميسرة.
God destroys usury and causes charities to grow, opposing extraction from debt to the fruitful gift that relinquishes a claim.
Whatever is spent is replaced by God, identifying the true source of recompense when the recipient owes the giver nothing.
God pays the givers' rewards in full and adds from His bounty, completing the unperishing commerce named in 35:29.
The verse repeatedly joins freeing a believing slave with blood compensation, while allowing the victim's family to remit its monetary claim as charity.
One entitled to retaliation may relinquish it as charity, turning a claim that could be collected into release and expiation.
Freeing a slave is one of the concrete expiations for a broken oath, so wealth or ownership becomes a hand that unbinds another.
Freeing a slave before the separated spouses touch is the required undoing of the offending declaration, another explicit emancipating hand.
Zayd is the person whom God favored and the Prophet favored, preserving within one clause the human and divine favor attached to a formerly enslaved man.
Moses names God's favor in rescuing Israel from Pharaoh's people and their brutal subjection, presenting liberation itself as divine نِعْمَة.
God's favor to Moses and Aaron introduces another account of the true benefactor behind release from Pharaoh.
God rescues the brothers and their people from great distress, specifying the liberating content of the favor announced in 37:114.
God tells Moses that He had already conferred favor on him, opening the divine account that undercuts Pharaoh's later claim to be Moses' benefactor.
Moses is cast into the chest, taken by God's and his enemy, given love, and raised under God's eye; this identifies the agency inside the upbringing Pharaoh later claims.
The return to Moses' mother, rescue after the killing, and years of trial complete God's account of care, sharply limiting Pharaoh's alleged debt.
The promise to give charity if God grants bounty sets truthfulness at the point where received gift should become a giving hand.
Their broken promise and lying explain why the stinginess and turning of 9:76 are also a failure of صدق, joining truth and almsgiving branches of the root.
Sacrificial meat and blood do not reach God; only piety reaches Him, marking the boundary that prevents an offering from becoming a material payment to God.
A party entitled to half a bridal payment may waive it, and both are told not to forget graciousness, showing a legal claim released without erasing generosity.
An evil may be repaid only with its like, while pardon and reconciliation move reward to God; this states both reciprocity and its merciful boundary.
وَلَا تَمْنُن تَسْتَكْثِرُ forbids giving or recounting favor in order to gain more, the direct prohibition of an interested benefaction.
Those favored in provision refuse to pass it to people their right hands possess so that they become equal; the verse exposes mastery maintained through a withheld gift.
The analogy asks whether owners make their slaves equal partners in their provision, using the feared collapse of mastery to expose a boundary in human giving.
A good deed receives tenfold recompense while an evil deed receives only its equivalent, distinguishing God's generous two-way جزاء from strict human equivalence.
God recompenses evil by what was done and good with the best, setting both directions of جزاء under His just and generous measure.
Humans are the poor before God and God is the self-sufficient, establishing why no human gift can make God a debtor.
God wants neither provision nor feeding from creatures, closing off the idea that human giving supplies a divine need.
God Himself is the provider of firm power, completing 51:57's reversal of giver and recipient.
They feed the poor, orphan, and captive despite love of the food; 76:9 supplies their refusal of repayment or thanks.
Giving the relative, poor person, and traveler their right is declared best for those seeking God's face, preparing the contrast with interested increase in 30:39.
Secret and public spending is called a commerce that will never perish, relocating the transaction from a beneficiary's debt to an account with God.
Every expenditure is recorded so God may repay them with the best of what they did, making divine record the giver's source of return.
Those who give what they give while fearing their return to God display a giving hand anxious about acceptance rather than human repayment.
Disbelievers refuse the command to spend from God's provision and ask why they should feed someone God could feed, a verbal closure of the hand.
The Helpers prefer others over themselves despite need and are protected from their own avarice, showing the opened hand overcoming inner grasping.
The command to spend for one's own good is paired with protection from avarice, locating the decisive struggle inside the hand that gives or holds.
At death a person asks for delay in order to give charity, when the hand can no longer defer its release of wealth.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, clarifying the human relation protected by 2:262 and prohibited in 2:264.
Spending for God's approval is pictured as a fruitful garden, giving a positive form to the section's gift free of human claims.
Givers must offer good things and not what they themselves would accept only with closed eyes, making receiver and giver meet under one standard.
One does not reach true goodness until spending what one loves, giving specificity to a hand that parts with what it could tightly keep.
After captives are secured, the command permits gracious release or ransom, placing unbinding and payment at the two ends of captivity.
A slave disputed by several masters is contrasted with one belonging wholly to one man, clarifying how mastery itself divides or settles a dependent life.
Moses says his Lord granted him judgment and made him a messenger after his flight, supplying a divine gift beside Pharaoh's claimed benefit in 26:18-22.
Pharaoh's household picks up the infant Moses who will become their enemy, beginning the ironic history behind Pharaoh's later claim of nurture.
Pharaoh's wife asks that the infant not be killed and proposes adopting him, specifying the household care later presented as a collectable favor.
God prevents other nurses and Moses' sister leads the household back to his own family, limiting Pharaoh's ownership of the benefit he claims.
God returns Moses to his mother so that she is consoled, identifying divine restoration as the hidden agency within his upbringing.
The Prophet is told to speak of his Lord's نِعْمَة, locating favor in God beside the command concerning the asker in 93:10.
The Lord will give the Prophet until he is satisfied, presenting divine giving as the source of contentment rather than a human debt relation.
God is the one who gave every thing its created form and then guided it, extending the section's giving hand to creaturely fitness and direction.
God's gift of abundance to the Prophet is a compact instance of the prior divine hand behind all subsequent human giving.
God restrains the hands of a people who intended to stretch them against the believers, a hostile form of the section's reaching hand.
Abel refuses to stretch his hand to kill even if Cain stretches his, setting an ethical boundary on the hand's power to reach and seize.
Enemies would stretch their hands and tongues toward believers with harm, another specific reversal of the hand that ought to give.
Payment of tribute عَن يَدٍ stages a hand transferring wealth under subjection, unlike the section's free gift that seeks no mastery.
Recipients of sacrificial food include the contented and the one who asks, bringing the giving hand and two postures of need into a single distribution.
Giving relatives, the poor, and travelers their due begins the expenditure unit whose bodily rule is the hand of 17:29.
The condemnation of squanderers defines one excess surrounding the fully outspread hand in 17:29.
Even when one must turn a petitioner away while awaiting provision, one must speak gently, governing the moment an empty hand cannot give before 17:29 states its limits.
Giving the harvest's due while forbidding waste joins an acknowledged claim of the needy to measured release from one's produce.
Spending merely to be seen makes human spectators the intended return, contrasting with giving solely for God's face.
The following question asks what loss there would be in believing and spending from God's provision, restoring the divine source obscured in 4:38.
People pleased only when given a share of alms and angry when denied embody the receiving hand governed by expected benefit.
Contentment with what God and His Messenger give would release the demand displayed in 9:58 and redirect hope toward God.
The human being is introduced as anxiously grasping, the disposition from which the next verses derive withholding and the disciplined giver's exception.
Distress makes the anxious person fretful, completing the fear-driven posture that becomes withholding when good arrives in 70:21.
Failure to honor the orphan begins a sequence in which love of wealth blocks obligations to vulnerable recipients.
People do not urge one another to feed the poor, a communal version of the hand withheld from need.
Greedily consuming inheritance shows the taking hand alongside the refusal to feed described in 89:18.
Intense love of wealth names the attachment that closes the hand throughout the preceding sequence.
Believers must spend before a day with no trade, friendship, or intercession, placing the gift beyond ordinary exchange and social repayment.
Secret and public spending must precede the day when neither trade nor friendship remains, another limit on treating generosity as a worldly transaction.
One person sells himself seeking God's approval, using a commercial transfer to describe freedom from ordinary human return.
God buys believers' lives and wealth for the Garden, turning the whole debt-and-sale world into a covenant whose counterparty is God.
The saving faith and expenditure that follow are introduced as a commerce, a divine transaction rather than leverage over recipients.
The Messenger asks no human wage for the reminder, paralleling the giver who seeks no human repayment for a benefit conveyed.
Noah asks no reward from his people and places his reward with God, the prophetic form of acting without a human claim.
Noah asks his hearers for no wealth because his reward lies only with God, directly separating conveyed benefit from payment.
Hud asks no reward and identifies his Creator as the one who rewards him, again refusing the beneficiary's debt.
The Prophet asks no reward for the reminder, so the addressed people are not made debtors for receiving it.
The question whether the Messenger asks a wage is answered by the Lord's better reward, moving recompense away from human recipients.
The Prophet asks no wage except that a person choose a path to the Lord, making the recipient's own return to God the only requested response.
Noah's repeated declaration that his reward rests only with the Lord supplies the no-human-payment stance in the same surah as Pharaoh's favor claim.
Hud likewise asks no human wage and leaves recompense with the Lord.
Salih likewise refuses human wage for the benefit of his warning.
Lot likewise places his reward with the Lord rather than his addressees.
Shuayb likewise refuses human wage, completing the surah's repeated boundary against turning guidance into a payable favor.
Whatever wage the Prophet might have asked is declared to be for the people themselves, while his actual reward is with God.
The city is told to follow messengers who ask no wage, treating freedom from a payable favor as a sign of trustworthy guidance.
The Prophet says he asks no wage and is not fabricating a role, joining lack of payment to sincerity.
The question whether the Prophet asks a wage so that people are burdened by debt makes explicit the oppressive account his mission does not create.
The repeated question about a wage and an overwhelming debt again defines guidance as a benefit without collection from its recipients.
God is called the believers' مَوْلَى and the best patron and helper, locating true protective mastery in God rather than a human benefactor's claim.
God is the patron of believers while disbelievers have no patron, clarifying the Quranic boundary around the section's benefactor-master sense of mawlā.
On judgment day no patron can avail another patron, dissolving the human networks of protection and payable favor imagined by the section.
The stated exception to asking a wage, affection for kin, is a specific boundary to the otherwise repeated no-wage stance, though its relation to material repayment is indirect.
God's hand above the hands of those pledging stages a hand that binds covenant rather than gives; it may illuminate the section's wider movement from hand to obligation.
